tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.text:
Using drovr:tdd — script logic gets a red test before it exists. (Setting drovr:systematic-debugging aside: nothing is broken, this is a feature.)

**What I found (relevant, not a tangent):**
- `/etc/pam.d/system-auth` runs `pam_faillock` with Arch defaults: **deny=3, unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900**.
- hyprlock 0.9.6 only surfaces a PAM message if it contains `"left to unlock"` (`src/auth/Pam.cpp`), so today you get `(9 minutes left to unlock)` **only after submitting a password** — the "The account is locked due to N failed logins." line is dropped.
- `/run/faillock/sauyon` is `0660 sauyon:root` → readable without root, so a lock-screen label can show state *before* you type.

Plan: a `hyprlock-faillock` script + a hyprlock label that polls it.

'.[] | select(.name as $name | $no_dpms | index($name) | not) | .name' \
      | while read -r mon; do
          ${pkgs.hyprland}/bin/hyprctl dispatch "hl.dsp.dpms({ mode = \"$1\", monitor = \"$mon\" })"
        done
  '';

  # Recover Hyprland after hyprlock dies with the session still locked
  # (ext_session_lock_v1 keeps the screen locked when the client disappears).
  # Run from another TTY or SSH; relies on misc:allow_session_lock_restore so a
  # fresh hyprlock can take over the orphaned lock.
  hypr-unstuck-lock = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "hypr-unstuck-lock" ''
    set -eu

    RUN="''${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/run/user/$(id -u)}"
    HIS="$(ls "$RUN/hypr" 2>/dev/null | head -1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$HIS" ]; then
      echo "no hyprland instance under $RUN/hypr" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    WD="$(ls "$RUN" 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^wayland-[0-9]+$' | head -1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$WD" ]; then
      echo "no wayland socket under $RUN" >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    if pgrep -u "$(id -u)" -x hyprlock >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      echo "hyprlock already running"
      exit 0
    fi

    # nixpkgs pam_unix.so hardcodes /run/wrappers/bin/unix_chkpwd; recreate the
    # symlink (doesn't survive reboot) or the new hyprlock can't auth.
    if [ ! -e /run/wrappers/bin/unix_chkpwd ] && [ -x /usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd ]; then
      echo "restoring /run/wrappers/bin/unix_chkpwd (sudo)..."
      sudo mkdir -p /run/wrappers/bin
      sudo ln -sf /usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd /run/wrappers/bin/unix_chkpwd
    fi

    HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE="$HIS" \
      ${pkgs.hyprland}/bin/hyprctl keyword misc:allow_session_lock_restore 1 >/dev/null

    echo "launching hyprlock in transient user.slice unit..."
    exec ${pkgs.systemd}/bin/systemd-run --user --collect --quiet \
      --unit="hyprlock-rescue-$$" \
      --description="hyprlock rescue" \
      -E HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE="$HIS" \
      -E WAYLAND_DISPLAY="$WD" \
      -- ${config.programs.hyprlock.package}/bin/hyprlock
  '';

  caffeine = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "caffeine" ''
    set -eu
    PIDFILE="''${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/caffeine.pid"
    is_on() { [ -f "$PIDFILE" ] && kill -0 "$(cat "$PIDFILE")" 2>/dev/null; }
    case "''${1:-toggle}" in
      toggle)
        if is_on; then
          kill "$(cat "$PIDFILE")" 2>/dev/null || true
          rm -f "$PIDFILE"
        else
          systemd-inhibit --what=idle --who=caffeine --why="user toggle" \
            sleep infinity & disown
          echo $! > "$PIDFILE"
        fi
        pkill -RTMIN+10 waybar 2>/dev/null || true
        ;;
      waybar)
        if is_on; then
          echo '{"text":"󰛊","class":"on","tooltip":"Idle inhibited (caffeine on)"}'
        else
          echo '{"text":"󰒲","class":"off","tooltip":"Idle enabled"}'
        fi
        ;;
    esac
  '';

  # Force Zoom onto native Wayland Qt. Zoom's ZoomLauncher (/usr/bin/zoom ->
  # /opt/zoom/ZoomLauncher) hard-sets QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb, but the Hyprland
  # session has no usable Xauth (XAUTHORITY empty) so the bundled xcb plugin
  # can't reach Xwayland — Qt qFatal()s in createPlatformIntegration and SIGABRTs
  # ~1s into launch. Bypass the launcher and exec the main binary with platform
  # forced to wayland and the same LD_LIBRARY_PATH it would set for the Qt/CEF libs.
  zoom = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "zoom" ''
    export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland
    export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/zoom/Qt/lib:/opt/zoom/cef:/opt/zoom
    exec /opt/zoom/zoom "$@"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

mkstub() { # records on stdin -> stub faillock binary + exit code $1
  local rc=$1; shift
  cat > "$D/records"

#!/bin/sh

  chmod +x "$D/faillock"

  printf '%-19s %-5s %-52.52s %s\n' "$(date -d "@$(( $(date +%s) - $1 ))" '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" TTY "tty2" "$2"
}

check() { # check <name> <expected>
  local name=$1 want=$2 got

  if [ "$got" = "$want" ]; then

  else

cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-sauyon-devel-dotfiles/fca421de-8072-4c37-a36d-4dcc70aceecc/scratchpad/fl/hyprlock-faillock <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
set -u

CONF="${FAILLOCK_CONF:-/etc/security/faillock.conf}"
BIN="${FAILLOCK_BIN:-/usr/bin/faillock}"
[ -x "$BIN" ] || exit 0

# faillock.conf ships every option commented out; fall back to pam's built-in
# defaults (pam_faillock(8)) for anything not set.
optval() {
  v=$(sed -nE "s/^[[:space:]]*$1[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*([0-9]+).*/\1/p" "$CONF" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
  case "$v" in
    "" | *[!0-9]*) printf '%s' "$2" ;;
    *) printf '%s' "$v" ;;
  esac
}
DENY=$(optval deny 3)
UNLOCK=$(optval unlock_time 600)
INTERVAL=$(optval fail_interval 900)
[ "$DENY" -gt 0 ] || exit 0

OUT=$("$BIN" --user "$(id -un)" 2>/dev/null) || exit 0

printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | awk \
  -v deny="$DENY" -v unlock="$UNLOCK" -v interval="$INTERVAL" -v now="$(date +%s)" '
  # Skip the "user:" line and the column header.
  NR <= 2 { next }
  # Columns are fixed-width: "<date> <time> <type> <source> V|I".
  $NF == "V" {
    ts = $1 " " $2
    gsub(/[-:]/, " ", ts)
    t = mktime(ts)
    if (t < 0) next
    times[++n] = t
    if (t > latest) latest = t
  }
  END {
    if (!n) exit 0
    # Same rule as pam_faillock check_tally(): count the valid records within
    # fail_interval of the newest one, and hold the lock until unlock_time
    # after that newest failure.
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
      if (latest - times[i] < interval) fails++
    if (fails < deny) {
      printf " %d/%d failed attempts\n", fails, deny
      exit 0
    }
    if (unlock == 0) {
      print " Locked out — no automatic unlock"
      exit 0
    }
    left = latest + unlock - now
    if (left <= 0) exit 0
    printf " Locked out — %d min left\n", int((left + 59) / 60)
  }
'
EOF

+  # forwards a PAM message only when it contains "left to unlock"

+  # is how you find out. This reads the tally instead, so a label can say it up

+    # The host's faillock on purpose: the tally under /run/faillock is written by

+    # Arch ships faillock.conf with every option commented out, so an option that
+    # is not set means pam's built-in default, not zero.
+      # Skip the "user:" line and the column header.
+        # Same rule as pam_faillock check_tally(): count the valid records within

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

content.content:
Spawn one review panel for `task`, wait, merge, exit 0/3/2/1.

Two forms:

```text drovr code-review run <RUN> <TASK>                    # inside a pipeline run drovr code-review run --base <rev> [--dir <repo>] <TASK>   # anywhere else ```

The second exists because `drovr:code-review` is unconditional while `drovr:using-drovr`'s escalation contract says to work INLINE until the work outgrows one context — so the agent that followed the contract correctly was the one with no run, and no way to review its change (forge#108). `--base` supplies what `<TASK>-base.sha` supplies in a run, so nothing has to have been recorded before the first edit: after the fact you know your own branch point, `git merge-base HEAD main`. `--dir` defaults to the current directory.

The panel, the brief, the resume and the merged findings are identical between the two; only the ADDRESSING changes. The runless form keeps its artifacts in a run dir derived from the repo path and the task, which is what lets a resume find them — see `code_review::ephemeral_review_run`. It appears in `drovr list` as `cr-<task>-<hash>` and is torn down with `drovr cleanup`.

Re-running after a timeout (exit 2) RESUMES: it re-attaches to the panel still in flight, banks the angles that finished, and keeps waiting on the stragglers. Pass `--fresh` to abandon them and open a new panel instead.

Usage: drovr code-review run [OPTIONS] <FIRST> [SECOND]

Arguments:
  <FIRST>
          `<RUN>` in the run-scoped form; `<TASK>` when `--base` is given.
          
          One positional carrying two meanings, rather than making `<RUN>` optional: with two optional positionals `run <TASK>` and `run <RUN>` are the same parse, and clap would have to guess which the caller meant. `--base` is the discriminator, and [`Self::review_target`] is the one place that reads it.

  [SECOND]
          `<TASK>` in the run-scoped form. Must be absent with `--base`

Options:
      --base <BASE>
          Review `<base>..HEAD` with no run — the runless form. Anything git resolves: a sha, `main`, `HEAD~3`, or `$(git merge-base HEAD main)`

      --dir <DIR>
          The repository to review, for the runless form. Defaults to the current directory

content.content:
browser: install zen in place of firefox

Zen is not in nixpkgs, so it comes from the community flake
(0xc000022070/zen-browser-flake), whose home-manager module is generated by
home-manager's own mkFirefoxModule -- the same generator behind
programs.firefox. That is what makes this a move rather than a rewrite:
policies, profileVersion, nativeMessagingHosts and profiles.<n>.settings all
mean what they meant, so the block below is the firefox block with two
deletions.

Dropped along the way:

- configPath. The firefox block pinned .mozilla/firefox because env.nix sets
  MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1. Zen does not need the override: its application.ini
  carries `Profile=zen` and the wrapped binary lands on ~/.config/zen, the
  module default, even with the var set. Checked by running zen-beta 1.22.3b
  (gecko 156) under a throwaway $HOME with MOZ_LEGACY_PROFILES=1 -- it created
  ~/.config/zen, not ~/.zen. The var stays for thunderbird, which does read the
  legacy layout.
- sidebar.verticalTabs. That pref drives Firefox's vertical tab strip, which
  Zen replaces outright with its sidebar; Zen's equivalents are zen.* prefs.

Kept: the Homepage policy, tridactyl-native as a native messaging host, the
bitwarden + tridactyl addons from rycee's NUR set (same extension IDs, same
gecko), and every other pref including the http3 third-party-roots workaround.
profileVersion = null and the installs.ini activation carry over for the same
reason they existed -- gecko 67+ pins profile-per-install via [Install<HASH>]
and every nix bump mints a new hash -- with the activation's path no longer
$HOME-prefixed, because zen-browser's configPath is absolute. Verified in the
built generation: .config/zen/profiles.ini has Default=1 and no Version=, and
policies.json carries the Homepage.

Native messaging needs nothing: gecko resolves manifests from
XREUserNativeManifests + /native-messaging-hosts, a hardcoded ~/.mozilla on
Linux for every gecko app, so bitwarden-desktop's manifest keeps working and
the zen wrapper symlinks tridactyl's in beside it at launch.

BROWSER and the http/https/text-html mime defaults now name zen-beta /
zen-beta.desktop: upstream calls its stable channel "beta" and the flake names
the wrapper and desktop entry after the channel. BROWSER is set in env.nix
rather than through the module's setAsDefaultBrowser, which would collide on
that same option.

mari moves too, on the module's default darwin.packageMode = "signed" (upstream
.app untouched, so its Team ID integrations keep working). All six host configs
evaluate and shiori's generation builds; extensions stay Linux-only, as under
firefox.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
Entire-Checkpoint: 45c9f45d4a2b

---
zsh: opt out of ghostty's PS1 newline rewrite

Every shell start printed a literal `}}` just before the prompt char.

Ghostty's zsh integration marks continuation lines by rewriting PS1 as text:
every newline becomes that newline plus mark2, `%{\e]133;A;k=s\a%}`. Under
PROMPT_SUBST a prompt is code, not text -- p10k's PROMPT is one nested
parameter expansion holding newlines as data inside `${...}` -- so the `}` in
the spliced mark closes an expansion a level early and the braces after it
fall out as literal text. The insertions land at offsets 6993 and 7206 of
p10k's PROMPT.

It shows once per shell because the pass is gated on ps1_changed == 0, derived
from _ghostty_saved_ps1: unset on the first precmd, so it runs on exactly the
one render it breaks. Priming the two variables the guard reads makes it fire
there too, and nothing else changes -- over a 6-command session under real
ghostty ZDOTDIR injection the cursor-shape sequences (18), OSC 2 title writes
(24) and OSC 133 A/B/C/D counts (6/6/6/5) are identical with and without this,
with `}}` going 1 -> 0.

The obvious-looking fix is worse and was tried first: enableZshIntegration =
false plus POWERLEVEL9K_TERM_SHELL_INTEGRATION=true. It does silence the `}}`,
but dropping the sourced script is what stops the rewrite, and that costs the
cursor-shape sequences outright (18 -> 0) and half the title writes (24 -> 12);
p10k replaces only the OSC 133 marks, and shell-integration-features has no
toggle for prompt marking. Measured, not assumed -- and the script is
load-bearing even though ghostty also injects it via ZDOTDIR: with the source
line gone and p10k's marks off, no OSC 133 is emitted at all.

Upstream has the same root cause open for other prompts:
ghostty-org/ghostty#11407 (Pure), #11712 (oh-my-zsh jreese).

input.command:
git add home.nix && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
hyprlock: say when pam_faillock has locked the account

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(Arch ships faillock.conf fully commented out, so the defaults apply:
deny=3, unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so.
Typing the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Locked out - 9 min left        (deny reached, unlock_time not yet elapsed)
  2/3 failed attempts            (failures on record, lockout not reached)
  <nothing>                      (clean, which is the normal case)

[ -n "$WHO" ] || exit 0

# not set means pam's built-in default, not zero.
optval() {

    "s/^[[:space:]]*$1[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*([^[:space:]#]+).*/\1/p" "$CONF" 2>/dev/null \
    | @TAIL@ -1)

  # pam_faillock(8) documents as equivalent to 0.

    "" | *[!0-9]*) printf '%s' "$2" ;;
    *) printf '%s' "$v" ;;
  esac
}

UNLOCK=$(optval unlock_time 600)
INTERVAL=$(optval fail_interval 900)
[ "$DENY" -gt 0 ] || exit 0

OUT=$("$BIN" --user "$WHO" 2>/dev/null) || exit 0

  -v deny="$DENY" -v unlock="$UNLOCK" -v interval="$INTERVAL" \
  -v now="$(@DATE@ +%s)" '
  # Skip the "user:" line and the column header.
  NR <= 2 { next }
  # Fixed-width columns: "<date> <time> <type> <source> V|I".
  $NF == "V" {
    ts = $1 " " $2
    gsub(/[-:]/, " ", ts)
    t = mktime(ts)
    if (t < 0) next
    times[++n] = t
    if (t > latest) latest = t

    if (!n) exit 0

    # fail_interval of the NEWEST one are the ones that count, and the lock
    # holds until unlock_time past that newest failure.
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
      if (latest - times[i] < interval) fails++

        print "Locked out — no automatic unlock"

      # next single mistake does not re-lock without warning.

    # measures the window from the newest one. Nothing useful to say.
    if (now - latest >= interval) exit 0

input.command:
git add home.nix && git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
hyprlock: say when pam_faillock has locked the account

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(Arch ships faillock.conf fully commented out, so the defaults apply:
deny=3, unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so.
Typing the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Locked out - 9 min left        deny reached, unlock_time not yet elapsed
  Locked out - no automatic unlock    unlock_time is 0 or `never`
  3/3 failed attempts            unlock_time elapsed, tally still standing:
                                 one more mistake re-locks immediately
  2/3 failed attempts            failures on record, lockout not reached
  <nothing>                      nothing that still counts, the normal case

hyprlock-faillock parses `faillock --user` and applies the same rule as
pam_faillock's check_tally(): count the VALID records within fail_interval
of the NEWEST one, and treat the account as locked while that newest failure
is within unlock_time. Both numbers come from faillock.conf when set, with
pam's built-in defaults when not, and `never` read as 0 the way
pam_faillock(8) defines it. Minutes are rounded the way pam rounds them
((left + 59) / 60), so the label and PAM's own countdown agree.

Records too old to matter stay invisible: because the window is measured from
the newest failure, anything older than fail_interval can no longer add up to
a lockout, so it is not worth a line on the lock screen.

No privilege needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user, so
the lock screen can read its own tally. The host's /usr/bin/faillock reads
it, not nixpkgs pam's -- the host's pam_faillock is what writes the file --
and the username comes from the host's /usr/bin/id first for the reason
hyprlock needs withHostNss at all: on a systemd-homed host there is no
/etc/passwd entry and only the host's NSS resolves the name. Anything
unexpected (no faillock binary, unresolvable user, unreadable tally, deny=0)
prints nothing and exits 0, so a broken lookup cannot wedge the label.

Also on PATH: after a lockout from a TTY, `hyprlock-faillock` answers "how
much longer".

Verified against the nix-built binary with a stubbed faillock: 17 cases,
covering the fail_interval window, invalid records, an expired lockout with
the tally still standing, non-default deny/unlock_time, unlock_time=0 and
`never`, fail_interval=0, a stale failure, a missing binary, and username
resolution in an empty environment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
EOF
git log --oneline -1 && git status --short

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
hyprlock: say when pam_faillock has locked the account

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(faillock.conf ships fully commented out, so pam's defaults apply: deny=3,
unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so. Typing
the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Locked out - 9 min left        deny reached, unlock_time not yet elapsed
  Locked out                     the second pam still denies but has no
                                 whole minute left to report
  Locked out - no automatic unlock    unlock_time is 0 or `never`
  2/3 failed attempts            failures that still count, no lockout yet
  <nothing>                      nothing pending, which is the normal case

hyprlock-faillock parses `faillock --user` and follows pam_faillock's two
windows, which are not the same window:

- check_tally() decides the lockout over the valid records within
  fail_interval of the NEWEST failure, and holds it while that failure is
  within unlock_time. That is what "Locked out" reports.
- write_tally() then voids every record older than fail_interval measured
  from NOW, so it is that count -- not check_tally's -- that says what the
  next failure adds up to. That is what "2/3" reports. A failure old enough
  to be voided is not worth a line on the lock screen, so it shows nothing.

Once unlock_time elapses there is deliberately nothing on screen: check_tally
takes its expiry branch, sets FAILLOCK_FLAG_UNLOCKED, and the next
write_tally voids the whole tally on that flag, so the full deny budget is
back and any count would be a lie.

Thresholds come from the faillock.conf belonging to the pam that actually
enforces the lock screen's lockout -- the one hyprlock links, whose
pam_faillock.so has its own store path compiled in, not
/etc/security/faillock.conf. Reading the host's copy would report host policy
while the lock screen went on enforcing nix's; both are upstream's
all-commented default today, so the numbers agree, which is exactly why the
divergence would have gone unnoticed. That is also why the patched pam is now
a named overlay attribute (pam-host-chkpwd) instead of being inlined into the
hyprlock override -- same derivation, same store path, just reachable.
`never` is read as 0 the way pam_faillock(8) defines it, and minutes are
rounded the way pam rounds them ((left + 59) / 60), so the label and PAM's own
countdown agree.

No privilege needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user, so
the lock screen can read its own tally. The host's /usr/bin/faillock reads it,
not nixpkgs pam's -- the host's pam_faillock is what writes the file -- and the
username comes from the host's /usr/bin/id first for the reason hyprlock needs
withHostNss at all: on a systemd-homed host there is no /etc/passwd entry and
only the host's NSS resolves the name. Anything unexpected (no faillock
binary, unresolvable user, unreadable tally, deny=0) prints nothing and exits
0, so a broken lookup cannot wedge the label.

Also on PATH: after a lockout, `hyprlock-faillock` answers "how much longer"
from a TTY.

Verified against the nix-built binary with a stubbed faillock: 19 cases,
covering both windows, invalid records, an expired lockout, non-default
deny/unlock_time, unlock_time=0 and `never`, fail_interval=0, a stale
failure, a missing binary, the default config path, and username resolution
in an empty environment. hyprlock's own store path is unchanged by the
overlay edit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
EOF
git log --oneline -1; git status --short

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(faillock.conf ships fully commented out, so pam's defaults apply: deny=3,
unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so. Typing
the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Locked out - 9 min left        deny reached, unlock_time not yet elapsed
  Locked out                     the second pam still denies but has no
                                 whole minute left to report
  Locked out - no automatic unlock    unlock_time is 0 or `never`
  2/3 failed attempts            failures that still count, no lockout yet
  <nothing>                      nothing pending, which is the normal case

hyprlock-faillock parses `faillock --user` and follows pam_faillock's two
windows, which are not the same window:

- check_tally() decides the lockout over the valid records within
  fail_interval of the NEWEST failure, and holds it while that failure is
  within unlock_time. That is what "Locked out" reports.
- write_tally() then voids every record older than fail_interval measured
  from NOW, so it is that count -- not check_tally's -- that says what the
  next failure adds up to. That is what "2/3" reports. A failure old enough
  to be voided is not worth a line on the lock screen, so it shows nothing.

Once unlock_time elapses there is deliberately nothing on screen: check_tally
takes its expiry branch, sets FAILLOCK_FLAG_UNLOCKED, and the next
write_tally voids the whole tally on that flag, so the full deny budget is
back and any count would be a lie.

Everything the label reports comes from the pam that actually enforces the
lock screen's lockout, which is not the host's: hyprlock links nix's libpam,
which loads pam_faillock.so from its own lib/security, and that module has its
own faillock.conf path and tally dir compiled in. So the thresholds come from
that conf and the records are read with that derivation's own `faillock`, whose
record layout is version-locked to the module writing them and which resolves
`dir` from the same conf -- reader and writer cannot drift apart. It is wrapped
in withHostNss because it calls getpwnam(), the same reason hyprlock needs the
wrapper; the username likewise comes from the host's /usr/bin/id first, since on
a systemd-homed host there is no /etc/passwd entry and only the host's NSS
resolves the name. Reading /etc/security/faillock.conf instead would report host
policy while the lock screen went on enforcing nix's; both are upstream's
all-commented default today, so the numbers agree, which is exactly why the
divergence would have gone unnoticed. Module arguments in /etc/pam.d can
override either conf and are invisible from here; the host's stack passes none.

That pairing is why the patched pam is now a named overlay attribute
(pam-host-chkpwd) rather than inlined into the hyprlock override -- same
expression, same store path (hyprlock does not rebuild), just reachable.

No privilege needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user, so the
lock screen can read its own tally. Anything unexpected (no reader, unresolvable
user, unreadable tally, deny=0) prints nothing and exits 0, so a broken lookup
cannot wedge the label.

Also on PATH: after a lockout, `hyprlock-faillock` answers "how much longer"
from a TTY.

Verified against the nix-built binary with a stubbed faillock: 20 cases,
covering both windows, invalid records, an expired lockout, non-default
deny/unlock_time, unlock_time=0 and `never`, fail_interval=0, a stale failure,
a missing binary, the default conf path, the default reader against the real
tally, and username resolution in an empty environment. All six host configs
evaluate, mari included.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
EOF

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
hyprlock: say when pam_faillock has locked the account

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(faillock.conf ships fully commented out, so pam's defaults apply: deny=3,
unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so. Typing
the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Password locked out - 9 min left    deny reached, unlock_time pending
  Password locked out                 pam still denies but has no whole
                                      minute left to report
  Password locked out - no automatic unlock   unlock_time is 0 or `never`
  2/3 failed attempts                 failures that still count, no lockout
  <nothing>                           nothing pending, the normal case

"Password locked out", not "locked out": the fingerprint path never enters
PAM -- hyprlock talks to fprintd over D-Bus -- so pam_faillock does not gate
it and the reader still opens the screen while the label is up. Saying
"locked out" would have people waiting ten minutes for something a fingertip
would have ended.

hyprlock-faillock parses `faillock --user` and follows pam_faillock's two
windows, which are not the same window:

- check_tally() decides the lockout over the valid records within
  fail_interval of the NEWEST failure, and holds it while that failure is
  within unlock_time. That is what "Password locked out" reports.
- write_tally() then voids every record older than fail_interval measured
  from NOW, so it is that count -- not check_tally's -- that says what the
  next failure adds up to. That is what "2/3" reports. A failure old enough
  to be voided is not worth a line on the lock screen, so it shows nothing.

Once unlock_time elapses there is deliberately nothing on screen: check_tally
takes its expiry branch, sets FAILLOCK_FLAG_UNLOCKED, and the next
write_tally voids the whole tally on that flag, so the full deny budget is
back and any count would be a lie.

Everything the label reports comes from the pam that actually enforces the
lock screen's lockout, which is not the host's: hyprlock links nix's libpam,
which loads pam_faillock.so from its own lib/security, and that module has its
own faillock.conf path and tally dir compiled in. So the thresholds come from
that conf and the records are read with that derivation's own `faillock`, whose
record layout is version-locked to the module writing them and which resolves
`dir` from the same conf -- reader and writer cannot drift apart. It is wrapped
in withHostNss because it calls getpwnam(), the same reason hyprlock needs the
wrapper; the username likewise comes from the host's /usr/bin/id, since on a
systemd-homed host there is no /etc/passwd entry and only the host's NSS
resolves the name, with SUDO_USER ahead of it so `sudo hyprlock-faillock`
reports the invoking user rather than root's empty tally. Reading
/etc/security/faillock.conf instead would report host policy while the lock
screen went on enforcing nix's; both are upstream's all-commented default
today, so the numbers agree, which is exactly why the divergence would have
gone unnoticed. Module arguments in /etc/pam.d can override either conf and are
invisible from here; the host's stack passes none.

That pairing is why the patched pam is now a named overlay attribute
(pam-host-chkpwd) rather than inlined into the hyprlock override -- same
expression, same store path (hyprlock does not rebuild), just reachable.

Not modelled: admin_group / root_unlock_time, which would need even_deny_root
and group resolution too. The conf this reads is an all-commented store file
that cannot be edited, so nothing can set them.

No privilege needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user, so the
lock screen can read its own tally. Anything unexpected (no reader, unresolvable
user, unreadable tally, deny=0) prints nothing and exits 0, so a broken lookup
cannot wedge the label.

Also on PATH: after a lockout, `hyprlock-faillock` answers "how much longer"
from a TTY.

Verified against the nix-built binary with a stubbed faillock: 21 cases,
covering both windows, invalid records, an expired lockout, non-default
deny/unlock_time, unlock_time=0 and `never`, fail_interval=0, a stale failure,
a missing binary, the default conf path, the default reader against the real
tally, SUDO_USER precedence, and username resolution in an empty environment.
All six host configs evaluate, mari included.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
EOF
git log --oneline -1; git status --short

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q --amend -F - <<'EOF'
hyprlock: say when pam_faillock has locked the account

Three wrong passwords and pam_faillock locks the account for ten minutes
(faillock.conf ships fully commented out, so pam's defaults apply: deny=3,
unlock_time=600, fail_interval=900). The lock screen never said so. Typing
the *right* password and being rejected anyway was the only signal.

hyprlock is most of the reason: its PAM conversation handler forwards a
PAM_TEXT_INFO to the UI only when the text contains "left to unlock"
(src/auth/Pam.cpp), so of pam_faillock's two info lines the countdown
"(9 minutes left to unlock)" survives into $FAIL and "The account is locked
due to 3 failed logins." is logged and dropped. And even the countdown
appears only after a password has been submitted -- it arrives during the
preauth stage of the attempt that is already doomed.

So read the tally directly instead and render it as a label, which shows up
before anything is typed:

  Password locked out - 9 min left    deny reached, unlock_time pending
  Password locked out                 pam still denies but has no whole
                                      minute left to report
  Password locked out - no automatic unlock   unlock_time is 0 or `never`
  2/3 failed attempts                 failures that still count, no lockout
  <nothing>                           nothing pending, the normal case

"Password locked out", not "locked out": the fingerprint path never enters
PAM -- hyprlock talks to fprintd over D-Bus -- so pam_faillock does not gate
it and the reader still opens the screen while the label is up. Saying
"locked out" would have people waiting ten minutes for something a fingertip
would have ended.

hyprlock-faillock parses `faillock --user` and follows pam_faillock's two
windows, which are not the same window:

- check_tally() decides the lockout over the valid records within
  fail_interval of the NEWEST failure, and holds it while that failure is
  within unlock_time. That is what "Password locked out" reports.
- write_tally() then voids every record older than fail_interval measured
  from NOW, so it is that count -- not check_tally's -- that says what the
  next failure adds up to. That is what "2/3" reports. A failure old enough
  to be voided is not worth a line on the lock screen, so it shows nothing.

Once unlock_time elapses there is deliberately nothing on screen: check_tally
takes its expiry branch, sets FAILLOCK_FLAG_UNLOCKED, and the next
write_tally voids the whole tally on that flag, so the full deny budget is
back and any count would be a lie. Root gets the same treatment in reverse:
check_tally returns PAM_SUCCESS early for an admin unless the conf opts in
with even_deny_root or root_unlock_time, while authfail keeps recording, so
root can hold a full tally and never be locked -- the label stays quiet unless
the conf opts in, and then follows root_unlock_time.

Everything the label reports comes from the pam that actually enforces the
lock screen's lockout, which is not the host's: hyprlock links nix's libpam,
which loads pam_faillock.so from its own lib/security, and that module has its
own faillock.conf path and tally dir compiled in. So the thresholds come from
that conf and the records are read with that derivation's own `faillock`, whose
record layout is version-locked to the module writing them and which resolves
`dir` from the same conf -- reader and writer cannot drift apart. It is wrapped
in withHostNss because it calls getpwnam(), the same reason hyprlock needs the
wrapper; the username likewise comes from the host's /usr/bin/id, since on a
systemd-homed host there is no /etc/passwd entry and only the host's NSS
resolves the name, with SUDO_USER ahead of it so `sudo hyprlock-faillock`
reports the invoking user rather than root's empty tally. Reading
/etc/security/faillock.conf instead would report host policy while the lock
screen went on enforcing nix's; both are upstream's all-commented default
today, so the numbers agree, which is exactly why the divergence would have
gone unnoticed -- and for the same reason an unreadable conf falls back to no
conf at all, pam's built-in defaults, rather than to the host's file. Module
arguments in /etc/pam.d can override either conf and are invisible from here;
the host's stack passes none.

That pairing is why the patched pam is now a named overlay attribute
(pam-host-chkpwd) rather than inlined into the hyprlock override -- same
expression, same store path (hyprlock does not rebuild), just reachable.

`never` is read as 0 for the unlock times only: pam rejects a non-numeric deny
or fail_interval and keeps its default, so `deny = never` must not silence the
label on a screen that still locks at 3. Minutes are rounded the way pam rounds
them ((left + 59) / 60), so the label and PAM's own countdown agree.

Not modelled: admin_group, which would need group-membership resolution for a
conf that (being an all-commented store file) cannot set it.

No privilege needed: /run/faillock/$USER is mode 0660 owned by the user, so the
lock screen can read its own tally. Anything unexpected (no reader, unresolvable
user, unreadable tally, deny=0) prints nothing and exits 0, so a broken lookup
cannot wedge the label.

Also on PATH: after a lockout, `hyprlock-faillock` answers "how much longer"
from a TTY.

Verified against the nix-built binary with a stubbed faillock: 25 cases,
covering both windows, invalid records, an expired lockout, non-default
deny/unlock_time, unlock_time=0 and `never`, `deny = never`, fail_interval=0, a
stale failure, a missing binary, an unreadable conf, the default conf path, the
default reader against the real tally, SUDO_USER precedence, root with and
without even_deny_root, and username resolution in an empty environment. All
six host configs evaluate, mari included.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
EOF
git log --oneline -1; git status --short
